Photograph: Ghanashyam Shrestha/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Relatives of people missing following flooding in Nepal visit Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Kathmandu, as they search for their loved ones. Photograph: Ghanashyam Shrestha/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Families balance hope and despair in race to find survivors in Nepal as 41 Australians still missing The walls of a teaching hospital are filled with pictures of unidentified victims as authorities collect DNA samples and plan burials before morgues fill up Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Cait Kelly in Kathmandu Sat 29 Aug 2026 20.27 EDT Last modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google S ome of them are young, some old; most of them appear to be men. Some of them could be sleeping, except for the mud that covers their bodies. Some, it seems, would be impossible to recognise even if you knew them well. Every few hours Nepalese authorities hang pictures of the deceased, who have not been identified, on a wall at the back of a teaching hospital in Kathmandu. Saluja, a young woman who did not give her last name, stood among a group of more than 100 people watching. Her cousin, 31, was not on the wall that day. “It’s very hard to identify their faces,” Saluja says. As she speaks, some in the crowd take videos to send to other relatives; they stand around comparing them, trying to work out whether the person in the photo is their loved one. The bodies have a piece of paper lying on top of them, showing which district they were found in, with a number to contact. “My cousin is missing,” Saluja says. “He worked in a hydro power plant … Since the flood, we have not been able to contact him. “It was the first area to get affected, so we really don’t know. But we are hoping for the best.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email While she talked, her other cousin, his older brother, was on the plane flying home from Australia. Since Wednesday, Kathmandu has swelled with international visitors – not tourists but people looking for their loved ones. The Nepalese government has deployed about 15,000 personnel – from the army to the police – to move up the valley and into the areas decimated by the flood, hoping to find survivors. View image in fullscreen A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding at the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in the Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP While they battle arduous search conditions – areas completely cut off, roads destroyed, bridges washed away and a new lake threatening to burst – loved ones from Australia rush to Nepal to be with their families. They come to chase leads and to wait. “My older cousin, he’s a doctor in Australia, and his wife is a dentist,” Saluja says. “So they both are coming back. They’re going to try with the search and to be with the family as well. They obviously want to be with the family.” It’s been four days since the glacier collapsed high in the Himalayas, sending a wall of water, ice and mud down to destroy everything in its path. The number of people killed has risen to 669, with nearly 3,000 people lost. On the Chinese side, more than 550 people are unaccounted for. Forty-two Australians are still missing, according to Dfat, including six identified as missing by Chinese authorities. On Saturday, New South Wales man Michael Keats was confirmed to be one of them. He had reached the Nepal-Tibet border just moments before disaster struck, his family said in a statement. View image in fullscreen Australian’s missing in Nepal. Clockwise from left - Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and Family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan. Composite: Supplied by the families “Confusion around the timing of the floods initially led us to believe our beautiful Michael would be safe in Kathmandu, preparing to fly home,” they said. “Unfortunately, it was confirmed relatively quickly by the Isha Foundation that Michael and his Kailash travel group had arrived at Gyirong Port on the Nepal-Tibet border just 10 minutes before the tragic floods hit.” Keats’ family said their thoughts and prayers were with everyone affected by the tragedy. “[Michael] is gentle and kind, with a unique light that touches everyone lucky enough to know him,” they said. Sagar Shrestha serves as the director of the Disaster and Crisis Management Department at the Nepal Red Cross Society in Kathmandu. He said the death toll could climb into the thousands. A map showing the flood zone in Nepal “But they are still finding survivors,” he says. “Some of them are being found in the jungle; they’ve gone up the mountain and are being helicoptered out.” He said there were 14 hydropower plants along the river, six of which were under construction. It’s believed people could still be alive in the majority of them. One of the key issues has become “the dignified management of the dead”, he says, as morgues and hospitals have filled up in some areas. According to local media, officials in the Chitwan district will collect DNA samples from 229 bodies that are starting to decay and are no longer identifiable, before burying them. “It is now the major concern,” Shrestha says. “And the second thing is that if we are not being able to manage the dead bodies, there could be some kind of health issues.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Morning Mail Our Australian morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Since the crisis started, Sagar Pandey has barely slept . Pandey, the chief executive of the Himalaya Glacier Company, says 47 people from the trekking service are lost, including 15 Australians. He had Australians in two different locations: five people 1.5km from the border of Tibet and Nepal, who were meant to be coming back that morning after breakfast and another 10 who had left the Syabrubesi valley and were driving towards the border checkpoint. “I believe they were trapped because all three cars and jeeps are missing,” he says. “There were a total of 14 people: three drivers and then one guide and 10 Australians.” How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more Pandey has been spending his days going between the hospitals and checking in with the morgues to see if anyone on his tours has shown up. He is contacting family members of loved ones who are overseas and helping those who have just arrived. He has also been grieving his brother, who was guiding one of the treks. On Wednesday, he chartered a helicopter to the disaster zone – he could see about 800 people standing on the mountain, who have all been rescued now, he says. “There is a very low chance of survival that someone can still be alive,” he says. “The next process is to find the body if possible.” There has been one glimmer of hope – on Saturday afternoon the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, announced Australian woman Cara Severino was found safe after consular officials worked out where she was, and reached her via four-wheel drive. View image in fullscreen Australian woman Cara Severino, who had been unaccounted for following the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border, was safely located. Photograph: Office of Senator Penny Wong In a statement, Severino said she got out safely by teaming up with other survivors and using a tractor to drive out of the national park. “My heart goes out to all the Nepalese families who are grieving loved ones,” she said. “We passed a guy hiking up to Thulu Safru who lost his whole family when their whole town was destroyed. It’s just so devastating and undeserving.” “I feel for the families of those still missing; I know how much my family and friends went through.” On Saturday afternoon, the Australian ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, was waiting at the airport. Six more members of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s crisis response team had just arrived to help. “There is a lot of damage to infrastructure, damage to power generation capability, damage to phone lines, telegraph poles, so communications is out,” he says. “Even the Nepali forces have lost contact with some of their personnel. “Given the nature of search, rescue, and recovery operations, there are people in the water, in the mud. They’re obviously in danger should further flooding occur, and we can get heavy rainfall at any time given the monsoon.” The disaster unfolded over three Nepalese districts – the one closest to Kathmandu has been the easiest to conduct search and rescue operations, because the accessibility is better and the valley is wider. Most Australians were last heard from in the top district, which was hit first by the flood. No one knows how long it will take to search the area and find everyone, Ernst says, but in the event an Australian is found, the embassy will be told immediately. “We understand that this is an incredibly difficult situation for [families],” Ernst says. “They should feel confident that the Australian government and the Nepalese government are doing everything we can to find their loved ones. “They are very welcome to maintain contact with the Department of Foreign Affairs through our contact numbers and our contact centre in Canberra. If they’re here in Kathmandu, they’re welcome to make contact directly with the embassy, including with me.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/25/saud.text: Saudi Arabia has intercepted ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis in Yemen after issuing warnings for several regions including Mecca, as France vowed to send "military means" to help shield the key Saudi oil terminal of Yanbu.The attacks were reported as fighting raged in Yemen between the Houthis and Riyadh-backed government forces, killing dozens of people on both sides, according to a tally from seven sources who spoke to the AFP news agency.The missiles were the latest in a series of escalating Houthi attacks since July, when renewed hostilities shattered a years-long truce and embroiled Yemen in the wider Middle East war.Since then, the Houthis have imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, hitting its tankers and territory and seizing swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast, which is vital for Saudi oil exports.Their gains cement the hold of Iran and its allies on the two waterways that the wider Gulf, including top crude exporter Saudi Arabia, relies on to ship out its oil and other fuel products.The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government since 2015 against the Houthis said six ballistic missiles had been intercepted, thwarting attacks on Taif and Yanbu."Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly," said coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki on X.Earlier, the Saudi Civil Defence had issued a brief series of alerts including one for Mecca, home to Islam's holiest sites, with separate warnings for the Red Sea governorate of Yanbu as well as the Taif, Jeddah and Tabuk regions.The alerts were lifted a few minutes later. In recent weeks, alerts have often preceded attacks by the Houthis.Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian denied that Tehran was directing Houthi battle plans."The Houthis are responsible for their own actions. They don't take directions from us as those who are resisting in the region, based on the situations that have been imposed on them," Pezeshkian told Fox News, according to the broadcaster's translation of his remarks.Pledge of support from FranceWith pressure mounting on Saudi Arabia, French President Emmanuel Macron said France planned to "send military assets, meaning soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect" Yanbu."Not to engage in any conflicts but to protect this site," Macron said in an interview with the television channels TF1 and France 2.The infrastructure in and around Yanbu forms a key node in Saudi Arabia's vast network of energy installations.Yanbu serves as the kingdom's primary crude export terminal on the Red Sea and is connected to its oil-producing regions near the Gulf coast by the East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline.Yanbu is also home to major oil storage and refining facilities, while its location on the Red Sea provides Saudi Arabia with an alternative route for sending crude and petroleum products towards European markets.Last week, Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca for the first time since 2017 with a drone that was downed, an accusation the group denied.A few days later, the group attacked the Saudi capital Riyadh, the first in years, marking a new escalation in the conflict.As the Houthi attacks targeted Saudi Arabia on Thursday, battles raged on the ground in Yemen.At least 150 Houthi fighters and government forces members have been killed in the past 24 hours, sources from both sides told AFP, including in clashes over hilltops overlooking the Bab al-Mandab strait at the mouth of the Red Sea.At least 98 soldiers and government forces members were killed, according to an AFP tally compiled from five military sources.Most were killed in Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, with dozens of Yemeni troops killed.The Houthis later claimed launching a complex barrage involving ballistic missiles and drones to target command centres and weapons depots in southern Saudi Arabia, with the group saying Yemeni and Sudanese fighters were killed and injured in the attack along with Saudi personnel.The group also claimed late on Thursday to have launched attacks across the border that targeted Aramco infrastructure in Yanbu and an unnamed site in Riyadh.At least 52 Houthi fighters were killed in other clashes, two sources from the group said.Many on both sides were also killed in clashes in the Kahboub Mountains and in areas between the Lahj and Taiz regions, as the Houthis seek to dominate the highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandab to protect newly seized territory.
